planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and plant into consistently moist to wet, loamy or clay soil, ideally sunk in a bottomless container to block runaway spread.

directions: Unlike the evergreen, rough-ridged scouring rush already common in cultivation, this species is smooth-stemmed and deciduous, dying back each winter for a useful textural and seasonal contrast in bog gardens and pond margins. It tolerates wet, sandy or gravelly soils poorly suited to most perennials across most of North America. Its dense rhizome mat is a genuine erosion-control asset along pond edges and streambanks but will crowd out shallow-rooted neighbors if not contained in a sunken barrier pot.

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in spring and plant into cool, consistently moist to wet, nitrogen-poor soil in part shade; grow in a sunken barrier pot unless a naturalized colony is the goal, since rhizomes travel freely.

directions: The only branched, feathery-looking horsetail in the genus, this species carries whorled, finely divided side-branches that give it a soft, almost conifer-seedling texture visually distinct from every jointed 'pipe-stem' horsetail already in cultivation. It is a genuine boreal and cool-temperate native suited to cold, wet woodland and bog settings, replicating the boggy conifer-forest understory and streambank habitats where it grows wild. It makes a good textural foil for ferns and hostas in a cold-climate shade or bog garden.
sources: US Forest Service Fire Effects Information System (FEIS)

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall or early spring onto a firm, weed-free seedbed, pressing seed into the surface for good seed-to-soil contact; mulch lightly with weed-free straw during establishment.

directions: This is the genuinely native North American equivalent that occupies the same open-meadow and lawn-edge niche as the non-native European woodrush, forming tidy, clump-forming, grass-like growth suited to naturalistic lawns, meadow edges, and sunny-to-part-shade rock garden plantings. Unlike the shade-loving woodrushes already common in cultivation, this species tolerates open meadow and lawn-edge conditions in full sun, making it a genuinely different-use native grass-like groundcover rather than a redundant shade filler. It forms neat, non-aggressive clumps well suited to low-mow native lawn mixes.

planting.note: Divide clumps or sow seed in spring into well-drained soil with some clay, rock, or sand content and a moderately acid pH, in part sun to light shade.

directions: Named for its distinctive bristly, hedgehog-like seed capsules, this woodrush adds a textural novelty absent from the smoother-seeded species already present in cultivation. It is genuinely more drought-tolerant than the shade- and bog-leaning woodrushes already in the collection, filling a dry-woodland-edge niche in mesic to dry forests over clay, rocky, or sandy acid soils. It spreads modestly by rhizome and naturalizes well at the dry edge of a woodland garden rather than in consistently moist beds.

planting.note: Divide the rhizome's offset storage bases in spring and plant into dry, acidic soil with rocky, sandy, or clay content and some shade.

directions: This woodrush's namesake feature — swollen, white, bulb-like storage tissue at the leaf bases — gives it genuine resilience in dry, acidic, infertile soils over chert, granite, or sandstone where moisture-loving woodrushes already in cultivation would fail. Plant it in dry, acidic, rocky or sandy soil with some shade, replicating its native upland-ridge and dry-slope habitat. It blooms early, from March through June, giving seasonal interest ahead of most other woodrush species, and rides out dry spells on its storage reserves better than irrigation-dependent companions.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall to let winter cold break dormancy naturally; irrigate regularly only through the first season, then reduce to little or no supplemental water.

directions: A Pacific Northwest native found from British Columbia to northern California west of the Cascades, this is the most sun-and-drought-tolerant woodrush available, suited to native plantings, rock gardens, or meadow edges rather than the deep-shade settings most woodrushes need. It is evergreen to summer-deciduous depending on moisture, and its tawny-black flower heads on wiry stems in spring give it a season of interest the shade-garden woodrushes in the collection don't share. Needs regular water only to establish, after which it thrives on winter rainfall alone.
